title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks (Complete Playbook)
author: Priya Shah
content:
Overview

This playbook consolidates serving runtime documentation for Redwood Inference: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, runtime runbooks, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for engineers operating, extending, and debugging the serving runtime and for on-call responders.

Goals
- Provide a single reference for architecture and operational procedures.
- Document kernel scheduling heuristics and knobs used in production.
- Standardize profiling and benchmarking methodology so results are comparable across releases and hardware.
- Provide runbooks for common incidents and escalation paths.

Audience
- Serving Runtime engineers, SREs, Performance engineers, and Solutions engineers working on Dedicated/Private deployments.

Contents (top-level)
1) Architecture overview
2) Kernel scheduling design and policies
3) Profiling playbook (how-to)
4) Benchmarking suite and standard workloads
5) Release notes (recent and notable changes)
6) Known issues & workarounds
7) Runtime runbooks (incident procedures)
8) Team wiki & contacts

1) Architecture overview

Summary:
The serving runtime is a low-latency, high-throughput inference engine composed of the following logical components: control plane, request router, worker pool (GPU agents), execution kernels, KV cache layer, batching layer, telemetry & tracing, and persistent model artifacts. The runtime supports heterogeneous hardware (A100/H100/TPU v4-like), quantized kernels, and model variants with automatic fallback routing.

Key components and responsibilities:
- Control plane: model catalog, rollout policies, decisioning for routing (latency vs cost), and config distribution. Ownership: Platform team.
- Request router: routes requests to appropriate worker pools by policy (latency, region, customer tier). Implements admission control and QoS. Ownership: Serving runtime core.
- Worker pool / GPU agents: run model shards/instances, manage KV cache, and serve tokens. Implements kernel selection and scheduling. Ownership: Serving runtime infra.
- Kernel selection & compilation: selects precompiled kernels or issues JIT compile based on model architecture and sequence-length profile. Uses a kernel cache keyed by model+quantization+seq-length-range.
- Batching & cache layer: continuous batching service with dynamic batch sizing and prefix/KV cache reuse to trade off latency/cost.
- Telemetry & tracing: emits per-request timing, kernel-level counters, GPU utilization, and memory metrics to observability.

SLOs and targets (production):
- Availability SLO: 99.95% per-region for hosted endpoints.
- Latency SLO (short prompts): p95 < 180ms, p99 < 350ms (subject to model/seq-length).
- Throughput target: tokens/sec per-GPU measured in benchmark suite.

2) Kernel scheduling design and policies

Overview:
Kernel scheduling decides when and where to execute model ops on GPU(s). The scheduler is kernel-aware (distinguishes attention, matmul, flash-attn variants) and workload-aware (batch size, sequence length, priority). It interfaces with the GPU agent to orchestrate kernel launches, memory planning, and KV cache prefetch/evict.

Scheduling primitives and concepts:
- Priority classes: real-time (interactive low-latency), standard (background/batched), background (offline rerank/embeddings).
- Batch buckets: buckets created by request characteristics (seq-length-range, model-variant, quantization) to maximize kernel efficiency while minimizing padding.
- Preemption & cooperative yielding: long-running background batches can be preempted by real-time work; preemption boundary aligned to micro-batches to reduce wasted progress.
- Kernel affinity: prefer kernels optimized for certain GPU arch (e.g., H100 kernels) and instruction sets.
- Staleness threshold: a maximum acceptable wait time (configurable per-priority) to avoid excessive tail latency from waiting for a full batch. Default staleness = 12ms for real-time buckets.
- Admission control: global token-based admission to prevent overcommit and protect p99. A request may be queued or rejected with backpressure depending on policy.

Tuning knobs (config table)
- realtime.max_batch_size: 8
- realtime.max_staleness_ms: 12
- standard.max_batch_size: 64
- standard.max_staleness_ms: 40
- background.max_batch_size: 256
- preemption.enabled: true
- kernel_affinity.prefer_arch: ["H100", "A100"]
- kvcache.prefetch_window: 2 (tokens ahead)

Example scheduling flow (numbered):
1. Router receives request, classifies into priority and bucket by model and seq-length.
2. Admission control checks tokens in flight for the customer/route.
3. Request is placed in bucket queue; batching timer starts.
4. If batch fullness or staleness threshold met, scheduler picks bucket and issues kernel launches across available GPUs.
5. Kernel affinity & memory planner select kernel variant.
6. On completion, telemetry emitted and result returned.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Goal: collect reproducible performance traces to analyze tail latency, kernel hotspots, memory pressure, and PCIe/host contention.

Tools:
- internal perf-trace collector (preferred)
- NVIDIA nsight-systems / nsight-compute (on H100/A100)
- nvprof (deprecated but available for older nodes)
- custom tracing (OTEL spans instrumented around batching and kernel launches)
- dmesg / nvidia-smi and GPU metrics

Profiling steps (operational):
1. Reproduce workload: use bench harness (see section 4) with the same model, quantization, and seq-length distribution.
2. Collect system-level metrics: GPU utilization, mem utilization, host CPU, NIC, and disk IO across the trial. Command: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 1
3. Capture kernel-level profile: run nsight-systems to capture kernel durations, launch latencies, and GPU-side stalls. Example: nsight-sys --capture-range=INTERNAL --output=trace.qdrep --target-pid <pid>
4. Collect runtime traces: enable perf-trace (config: sampling=5ms, include-kernel-spans=true).
5. Correlate traces: map OTEL spans to kernel launches and queuing delays.
6. Triangulate root cause: look for (a) batching starvation (low math utilization with many small kernels), (b) memory thrashing / OOM, (c) PCIe stalls due to host-side copying, (d) suboptimal kernel variant selection.

Profiling checklist (quick):
- Reproducible input set captured (prompt corpus + seed).
- Bench harness config saved alongside trace.
- GPU metrics (nvidia-smi) for the full run.
- nsight trace file attached to ticket.
- Annotated p50/p90/p99 token latency table.

4) Benchmarking suite and standard workloads

Purpose: provide consistent, automated benchmarks for per-release performance regressions, hardware comparisons, and tuning. Benchmarks are runnable locally in CI and in lab cluster.

Standard workloads (examples):
- interactive-short: seq_len 16-64, request-per-second bursty, model family: small -> base models (LLM-7B).
- interactive-medium: seq_len 128, model family: 13B.
- long-context: seq_len 2048-8192, model family: 33B+, focus on KV cache effectiveness.
- embeddings-throughput: bulk embedding ingestion workload with batch semantics.
- rerank-latency: small model with many short queries (aim to optimize p99).

Benchmark config table (sample):
- model: redwood-13b-int8
  hardware: H100 80GB
  batch_sizes: [1,4,8,16]
  seq_lengths: [32,128,512]
  metrics: tokens/sec, p50/p90/p99 latency, GPU_util, mem_used

- model: redwood-70b-qat
  hardware: A100 80GB
  batch_sizes: [1,2,4,8]
  seq_lengths: [256,1024,4096]
  metrics: same as above

Running the benchmark (example CLI):
- ./bench/run_bench --model redwood-13b-int8 --hardware h100 --workload interactive-medium --duration 10m --output ./results/run-2028-01-12.json

Bench outputs saved to: s3://redwood-bench-results/<date>/<run-id>. Include the bench config with each run. CI gating: major PRs to serving runtime must not regress p95 by >5% on interactive-short.

5) Release notes (summary of recent changes)

2028-01-12 Release (v2028.01.12) - published
- Kernel selection: introduced sequence-length-aware kernel cache. Result: ~20% p99 reduction for mixed-length workloads.
- Scheduler: default realtime.max_staleness_ms lowered from 16ms to 12ms to tighten p99.
- Profiling tooling: perf-trace v2; improved OTEL integration for kernel spans.
- Benchmarking: added long-context workload with seq_len up to 8192 and KV cache hit-rate telemetry.
- Fixed: a race in KV cache eviction causing transient OOMs during scale-down.

Planned next milestones:
- Q1 2028: adaptive batching experiment (per-customer SLA-aware batching).
- Q2 2028: precompiled kernel registry for common quantization profiles.

6) Known issues & workarounds

Issue: p99 spikes for mixed short+long workloads on A100 nodes
- Symptom: intermittent p99 increases by 2-3x under mixed traffic.
- Root cause: kernel fragmentation — small tasks interleaved with large kernels reduce concurrency.
- Workaround: pin heavy long-context requests to dedicated standard pools (route-by-seq-length).
- Fix: ongoing (adaptive kernel coalescing work).

Issue: occasional model load OOM during rolling upgrades
- Symptom: worker OOMs when model versions changed on nodes with fragmented memory.
- Workaround: set model-load-buffer to 0.2 (reserves 20% memory) and perform staged rollout with drain window 300s.

Issue: NVLink peer-to-peer fallback on older infra
- Symptom: traffic falls back to PCIe leading to throughput loss.
- Workaround: prefer colocated HBM-backed nodes for throughput-critical pools; set kernel_affinity.prefer_arch to avoid affected nodes.

7) Runtime runbooks (incident procedures)

A. High p99 latency (interactive workloads)
1. Triage: check global dashboard for affected routes/models.
2. If >3 routes affected, escalate to Platform SRE and create INCIDENT channel #inc-serving-runtime.
3. Run quick health checks: 
   - nvidia-smi on suspect nodes (look for 100% util & high mem).
   - Check admission rates and queue lengths in router.
4. If queueing delays high: reduce realtime.max_staleness_ms temporarily to 6ms and/or lower admission rate for lower-tier tenants.
5. If kernel hotspots identified: attach nsight trace and consult kernel-owner (see contacts).
6. Restore config changes via canary before global rollout.

B. OOM on worker node
1. Mark node as unschedulable (cordon).
2. Drain non-critical pools; capture kernel logs and dmesg.
3. If modelload caused OOM: rollback last model version or reduce concurrency for that model.
4. Increase model-load-buffer or add swap-backup for on-prem nodes as temporary mitigant.

C. Degraded throughput / GPU underutilization
1. Check batch sizes reported by telemetry. Low batch sizes often indicate misbucketed requests.
2. Validate seq-length distribution; if heavy variance, enable per-route bucketing by seq-length.
3. Run bench harness against node to reproduce and collect nsight trace.

D. Deployment rollback procedure (safe rollback)
1. Open deployment in control plane and pause rollout.
2. Roll back model binary and kernel registry versions to last-known-good.
3. Drain and restart affected worker pool one pod at a time.
4. Monitor p95/p99 for 30 minutes before unpausing.

Escalation matrix and contacts
- On-call serving runtime (primary): @oncall-serving-runtime (Slack, pages via PagerDuty)
- Kernel owners: @kernel-team (kernel-specific escalation)
- Platform SRE: @platform-sre
- Incident commander: rotate per incident (see team wiki contact page)

8) Team wiki & contacts

Where to find more granular docs and artifacts:
- Team wiki index: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki (this page links to playbooks, runbooks, and bench results).
- Bench results bucket: s3://redwood-bench-results/ (internal access only).
- Traces and nsight files: traces://redwood-traces/<run-id> (access via internal tooling).

Ownership & maintenance
- Document owner: Priya Shah (serving-runtime perf & infra).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major release affecting kernel scheduling.
- CI gates: perf regression checks enforced on main branch for interactive-short workload.

Appendix A — Example configs (YAML-like snippet)

# scheduler.yaml
realtime:
  max_batch_size: 8
  max_staleness_ms: 12
  priority: 100
standard:
  max_batch_size: 64
  max_staleness_ms: 40
  priority: 50
background:
  max_batch_size: 256
  max_staleness_ms: 200
  priority: 10
preemption:
  enabled: true
  boundary_micro_batches: 2

Appendix B — Quick commands
- nvidia-smi live: nvidia-smi -l 1 --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv
- run bench: ./bench/run_bench --model redwood-13b-int8 --workload interactive-short --duration 600
- collect perf-trace: perf-trace collect --pid <pid> --sampling-ms 5 --out ./trace.zip

If you find missing material, please file a documentation ticket and assign to the author. For urgent incidents, follow the runbook steps and page the on-call channel.
